extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, curriculum designers, and administrators responsible for quantitative reasoning/quantitative literacy programs and course instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Institutional guidelines for a college-level Quantitative Reasoning (QR) program: the two-part requirement (basic skills + overlay), the target QR skills, assessment formats and passing rules, design objectives for overlay courses, minimum topical exposure for overlays, and recommended pedagogical/administrative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: M101 course outline (five sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text provides the course outline in five sections: statistics; logical reasoning; geometry in problem solving; estimation, approximation, and judging the reasonableness of answers; and problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics occupies about one third of the course and includes measures of central tendency and dispersion, the normal curve, sampling, probability, and the nature of statistical testing. Geometry includes graphical solution of polynomial equations, systems, and spatial relationships. The algebra/analysis section includes function concept, average rate of change, and error analysis. The problem-solving section includes frameworks and an introduction to exponential functions for personal business problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and assessment practices for competency course
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate transfer to students' lives, avoid artificial situations, model the problem solving framework throughout instruction, and explicitly mention it early in the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an upbeat attitude, accommodate diverse learning styles, and evaluate students not only by hour exams and a final but also by homework, weekly quizzes (including written explanations), and project work. Use team projects (groups of four) with required individual written reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course coordinator responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the seven courses is assigned a course coordinator who prepares a uniform syllabus, advises instructors, prepares the departmental final exam, and works with GTAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course coordinator (often a master teacher) prepares homework sheets and project forms for all sections, helps faculty and GTAs understand the competency philosophy, and supports consistent grading and instruction across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mixed assessment and value-added measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment studies include pre/post comparisons (a 'starter's quiz' at the first week and comparable items on the final) to measure student learning gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value-added tabulations typically show at least a 25% improvement; other longitudinal analyses (e.g., grade correlations two years later) can evaluate grading standards and predictive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part QR requirement (basic skills + overlay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wellesley’s QR requirement has two components: the 'basic skills' component and the 'overlay' component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students satisfy the basic skills component by passing the QR Assessment on entry or by passing a basic skills course in the first year; they must also pass a QR overlay course to gain in-depth disciplinary experience with data analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR skill area: reading and understanding quantitative information
rubrics_metrics.description: (MAA skill 1) Reading and understanding quantitative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the basic skills students should develop and be assessed on; covered in QR basic skills course and expected for overlay eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR skill area: interpreting quantitative information and drawing appropriate inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: (MAA skill 2) Interpreting quantitative information and drawing appropriate inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize interpretation in contexts (medical decisions, personal finance) and in overlay courses that teach discipline-specific data analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR skill area: solving problems
rubrics_metrics.description: (MAA skill 3) Solving problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach problem formulation and solution in authentic contexts rather than rote procedures; model problem-solving framework throughout instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR skill area: estimating answers and checking for reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: (MAA skill 4) Estimating answers and checking for reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include estimation and error/relative-error analysis in course topics and assignments to build judgment about plausibility of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR skill area: communicating quantitative information
rubrics_metrics.description: (MAA skill 5) Communicating quantitative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require written explanations (e.g., weekly quiz questions expecting written answers) and individual written project reports to develop communication skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR skill area: recognizing limits of mathematical/statistical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: (MAA skill 6) Recognizing the limits of mathematical or statistical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach when models/procedures apply, sampling limitations, biases, and interpretations so students understand the bounds of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR Assessment format and passing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment consists of eighteen questions requiring written answers (not multiple choice). Students receive full credit, half credit, or no credit on each question. A score of 9.5 or better is needed to pass the assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students score between 9.5 and 12.0 may opt to take the basic skills class to improve skills; students who do not pass must enroll in the basic skills course. Students are permitted two successive opportunities to take the assessment upon arrival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic skills course structure (QR 140) and prerequisite policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic skills course was expanded from a ten-week half-credit to a full-semester, full-credit course designated QR 140; fulfillment of the basic skills requirement is a prerequisite for many quantitative courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are normally required to satisfy the basic skills component in their first year; QR140 is intended for students who did not pass the entry assessment and aims to raise both skills and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay objective A — Literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Literacy: The number of topics and the depth of coverage should be sufficient to ensure that students have the basic knowledge they need in order to function in real-life situations involving quantitative data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlay courses must provide enough topical breadth/depth so graduates can operate with quantitative data in practical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay objective B — Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity: Students should have experience in using authentic numerical data. The experience should arise naturally in the context of the course and actually advance the work of the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data analysis tasks should use real data tied to course goals (not artificial exercises) to realize literacy and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay objective C — Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicability: The examples used in an overlay class should be adequate to convince the average student that the methods used in the analysis of data are of general applicability and usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select examples that demonstrate how methods transfer to other contexts; ensure students see wider usefulness beyond narrow cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay objective D — Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding: A student’s experience with data analysis should not be limited to rote application of some involved statistical procedure. Rather, students should understand enough of what they are doing so that their experience of data analysis is likely to stay with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach conceptual foundations, interpretation, and judgment, not just mechanics, so skills persist as 'residue of judgment' for future analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay objective E — Practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicality: The breadth of topics covered and the depth of coverage should be consistent with what an average Wellesley student can realistically absorb in a course that devotes only part of its time to data analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance ambition with realistic workload and time constraints of an overlay course; prioritize key topics that achieve literacy and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Framework for Data Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework for Data Analysis: Provide an overview of how empirical questions/hypotheses can be raised, how relevant data can be collected and analyzed, and what conclusions these data allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should formulate answerable questions, decide what data to collect and how, perform analysis, and interpret conclusions relative to the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Collecting Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting Data: Address issues of data quality—representativeness vs bias—and relevance of collected data to the question being investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover random samples, experiments vs observational studies, blind/double-blind designs, and other design issues affecting validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Representing Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing Data: Stress different methods of representing data—numerical (tables), visual (pie charts, scatter-plots, line graphs, histograms), and verbal (reasonable captions describing a graph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach proper selection and labeling of graphical/numeric displays and how to write informative captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Summarizing Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarizing Data: Expose students to different ways of summarizing data, including verbal summaries and measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and dispersion (range, standard deviation, percentiles, indexes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss what measures communicate about a distribution and when particular summaries are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability: Students should have some understanding of basic probability, including addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability, and vocabulary of independence and mutual exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure working knowledge of when and how to apply rules and interpret probabilistic statements in data contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributions: Work with examples of different distributions (normal and non-normal), know when to expect normality, what skewness means, and that a normal distribution is specified by mean and standard deviation and percentages determined from tables/formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach interpretation of mean/median/SD, detection of skewness, and use of normal tables/formulas for proportion calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum exposure: Sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Sampling: Discuss sampling and stress the distinction between 'sampling' and 'collecting data.' Introduce sample mean and why it may vary from the population mean; emphasize distinction between sample statistics and population parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach sampling variability, sampling error, and implications for inference and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic application: Issues Regarding Sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one application should address issues regarding sampling, including how to obtain a random sample and how to detect sample biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic sampling problems that reveal potential biases and practical obstacles to representative sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic application: Making and Justifying Inferences from Data
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one application could address making and justifying inferences from data, including confidence intervals and hypothesis tests and exploring how one determines whether measured variation cannot plausibly be attributed to chance alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach conceptual basis of inference, interpretation of p-values/confidence intervals, and limits of conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic application: Regression Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one application could study methods for fitting curves to data and for analyzing deviations of the data from these curves (regression analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include model fitting, residual analysis, and interpretation of model fit and predictive limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay course designation and distribution credit (overlay concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'overlay' indicates students may use one of the designated QR courses to simultaneously satisfy another of the College’s distribution requirements (e.g., Natural and Physical Science Requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlay designation allows integration of QR objectives into disciplinary courses; course proposals should show how QR objectives are met while also serving distributional goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight, coordination, and continuous improvement for overlay courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the QR Program are committed to meeting with department chairs and instructors of QR overlay courses at least annually to ensure continuing quality; planned improvements include an annual workshop for overlay instructors and a QR Program web site to make guidelines accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require periodic review, shared resources/workshops, and centralized guidance to maintain consistent quality as courses and instructors change.
